claim: 70 communities in Bangladesh were randomly selected from 97,162 communities in the national census, with probability of selection proportional to community population size.
source: We randomly selected 70 communities from the 97,162 communities in the national census, where the probability of selection was proportional to the size of the community population.
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section describing the sampling procedure.

claim: Study teams visited each selected community at least twice, once during 08/2014-12/2014 (Y1) and once during 10/2015-01/2016 (Y2).
source: Study teams visited each of the selected communities at least twice, once during the period 08/2014-12/2014 (Y1) and once during the period 10/2015-01/2016 (Y2) to conduct interviews, collect serum and trap mosquitoes.
evidence: Direct statement describing the study timeline and visit schedule.

claim: 5866 individuals fully participated in the study across 70 communities.
source: In total, 5866 individuals fully participated (completed questionnaire and had blood taken) in our study across 70 communities, 2911 during August–December 2014 and 2955 during October 2015 – January 2016 (Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement of the total number of participants.

claim: 24% of individuals had evidence of past dengue infection.
source: We found that overall, 24% of individuals had evidence of a past infection.
evidence: Direct statement of the overall seroprevalence finding.

claim: 27% of males were seropositive compared to 21% of females (p-value<0.001).
source: We observed substantial heterogeneity by age and sex (Figure 1B), with 27% of males seropositive compared to 21% of females (p-value<0.001).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical comparison between sexes.

claim: Individuals > 20 years had 30% seropositivity compared to 14% in those under 20 years.
source: Individuals > 20 y had 30% seropositivity compared to 14% in those under 20y.
evidence: Direct statement comparing seropositivity by age group.

claim: There was close correlation (Pearson correlation of 0.92) between the proportion seropositive in a community between 2014 and 2015.
source: There was close correlation between the proportion seropositive in a community between 2014 and 2015 (Pearson correlation of 0.92) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical measure and reference to figure.

claim: There was no observed difference in seropositivity across the two years of the study (p=0.66).
source: Overall, there was no observed difference in seropositivity across the two years of the study (p=0.66).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical test result.

claim: 91% of the study population aged >10 years had heard of dengue.
source: While most of the study population (91%) aged >10 y had heard of dengue, only 38 individuals (0.6%) reported having had dengue, of whom only 16 had evidence of past infection.
evidence: Direct statement of awareness levels in the study population.

claim: Only 38 individuals (0.6%) reported having had dengue, of whom only 16 had evidence of past infection.
source: While most of the study population (91%) aged >10 y had heard of dengue, only 38 individuals (0.6%) reported having had dengue, of whom only 16 had evidence of past infection.
evidence: Direct statement comparing self-reported dengue to serological evidence.

claim: Seropositivity ranged from 3% in rural Maulvibazar in Sylhet Division to 88% in urban Chittagong.
source: While all communities had at least one seropositive individual, there was substantial spatial heterogeneity across the country with the proportion seropositive ranging from 3% in rural Maulvibazar in Sylhet Division to 88% in urban Chittagong.
evidence: Direct statement describing the range of seropositivity across locations.

claim: Communities in the northern division of Rangpur had a mean seropositivity of 9% compared to 45% for communities in Khulna division in the southeast.
source: Communities in the northern division of Rangpur had a mean seropositivity of 9% compared to 45% for communities in Khulna division in the southeast.
evidence: Direct statement comparing seropositivity between divisions.

claim: Males had 1.6 times the unadjusted odds (OR: 1.6 [95%CI: 1.4–1.9]) and 1.7 times the adjusted odds (aOR: 1.7 [1.5–2.0]) of being seropositive compared to females.
source: In particular, males were much more likely to be seropositive (odds ratio [OR]: 1.6 [95%CI: 1.4–1.9]; adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 1.7 [1.5–2.0])
evidence: Direct statement with regression analysis results.

claim: Those who had travelled in the prior 7 days had twice the unadjusted odds (OR: 1.9 [1.5–2.4]) and 1.4 times the adjusted odds (aOR: 1.4 [1.1–1.8]) of being seropositive compared to those that had not travelled in the prior 6 months.
source: Travel also appeared important, with those who had travelled in the prior 7 days having twice the odds of being seropositive compared to those that had not travelled in the prior 6 months (OR: 1.9 [1.5–2.4]; aOR: 1.4 [1.1–1.8]).
evidence: Direct statement with regression analysis results.

claim: Household-level covariates including electricity, access to clean water, land ownership, and household income were not associated with seropositivity.
source: Household-level covariates did not appear to be important in determining risk of seropositivity, including having household electricity, household access to clean water, land ownership or household income.
evidence: Direct statement of regression analysis findings for household-level factors.

claim: The use of mosquito control in the household was not associated with seropositivity (OR: 0.9 [0.8–1.1]; aOR: 0.9 [0.7–1.1]).
source: The use of mosquito control in the household was also not associated with seropositivity (OR: 0.9 [0.8–1.1]; aOR: 0.9 [0.7–1.1]).
evidence: Direct statement with regression analysis results.

claim: Individuals living in locations where Ae. aegypti was found had higher odds of being seropositive (OR 1.8 [1.2–2.8], aOR 1.4 [0.9–2.2]).
source: At the community-level, we found some evidence that individuals living in locations where we had found Ae. aegypti were more likely to be seropositive, although this effect was less in the multivariable model (OR 1.8 [1.2–2.8], aOR 1.4 [0.9–2.2]).
evidence: Direct statement with regression analysis results.

claim: Having Ae. albopictus in the community was not linked to individual serostatus (OR 1.1 [0.7–1.6], aOR 1.0 [0.7–1.6]).
source: Having Ae. albopictus in the community was not linked to individual serostatus (OR 1.1 [0.7–1.6], aOR 1.0 [0.7–1.6]).
evidence: Direct statement with regression analysis results.

claim: Ae. aegypti was found in 23 (33%) of communities.
source: Overall Ae. aegypti was found in 23 (33%) and Ae. albopictus in 29 (41%) of communities with a slight negative correlation between the two (Pearson correlation of −0.2, p-value 0.07).
evidence: Direct statement of mosquito surveillance findings.

claim: Ae. albopictus was found in 29 (41%) of communities.
source: Overall Ae. aegypti was found in 23 (33%) and Ae. albopictus in 29 (41%) of communities with a slight negative correlation between the two (Pearson correlation of −0.2, p-value 0.07).
evidence: Direct statement of mosquito surveillance findings.

claim: There was a slight negative correlation (Pearson correlation of −0.2, p-value 0.07) between Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus presence.
source: Overall Ae. aegypti was found in 23 (33%) and Ae. albopictus in 29 (41%) of communities with a slight negative correlation between the two (Pearson correlation of −0.2, p-value 0.07).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical measure of correlation.

claim: The median seropositivity in communities with Ae. aegypti was 33% compared to 13% in communities without it.
source: The median seropositivity in communities with Ae. aegypti was 33% compared to 13% in the other communities.
evidence: Direct statement comparing seropositivity by mosquito presence.

claim: The median seropositivity in communities with Ae. albopictus was 15% compared to 18% in communities where it was not found.
source: The median seropositivity in communities with Ae. albopictus was 15% compared to 18% in communities where it was not found.
evidence: Direct statement comparing seropositivity by mosquito presence.

claim: Each unit increase in log population size was associated with a 1.3 times increased probability of being seropositive (95% CI: 1.2–1.5).
source: Individuals living in urban communities were more likely to be seropositive than those living in rural communities with each unit increase in log population size associated with a 1.3 times increased probability of being seropositive (95% CI: 1.2–1.5).
evidence: Direct statement with regression analysis results.

claim: The Matern spatial covariance matrix explained 15% of the variance in individual level responses.
source: The intraclass correlation coefficients showed that the Matern spatial covariance matrix explained 15% of the variance, the community-level random effects explained 6% and the household random intercept explained 12% of the variance in individual level responses.
evidence: Direct statement of variance partitioning from statistical model.

claim: The community-level random effects explained 6% of the variance in individual level responses.
source: The intraclass correlation coefficients showed that the Matern spatial covariance matrix explained 15% of the variance, the community-level random effects explained 6% and the household random intercept explained 12% of the variance in individual level responses.
evidence: Direct statement of variance partitioning from statistical model.

claim: The household random intercept explained 12% of the variance in individual level responses.
source: The intraclass correlation coefficients showed that the Matern spatial covariance matrix explained 15% of the variance, the community-level random effects explained 6% and the household random intercept explained 12% of the variance in individual level responses.
evidence: Direct statement of variance partitioning from statistical model.

claim: Including spatial covariance was associated with a small improvement in model fit (Deviance Information Criterion [DIC] difference of 4).
source: Including spatial covariance was associated with a small improvement in model fit, justifying its inclusion (Deviance Information Criterion [DIC] difference of 4).
evidence: Direct statement of model comparison results.

claim: Approximately 25% (95% CI: 21–29%) of the population had been infected with dengue at some point during their lives.
source: Overall, we estimate that approximately 25% (95% CI: 21–29%) of the population had been infected with dengue at some point during their lives, equivalent to 40.3 million individuals (95% CI: 34.3–47.2).
evidence: Direct statement of estimated national burden from spatial prediction model.

claim: 40.3 million individuals (95% CI: 34.3–47.2) in Bangladesh had been infected with dengue at some point during their lives.
source: Overall, we estimate that approximately 25% (95% CI: 21–29%) of the population had been infected with dengue at some point during their lives, equivalent to 40.3 million individuals (95% CI: 34.3–47.2).
evidence: Direct statement of estimated national burden from spatial prediction model.

claim: The proportion of people seropositive in communities was spatially correlated up to 108 km.
source: We found that the proportion of people seropositive in communities was spatially correlated up to 108 km (as measured from the Matern covariance function), consistent with that observed in a variogram of the seropositivity between communities (Figure 2B).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to spatial analysis and figure.

claim: The spatial prediction model performed well at estimating observed levels of seropositivity with a Pearson correlation of 0.8 between observed and fitted values and a mean absolute error of 8%.
source: Our model performed well at estimating the observed levels of seropositivity in participating communities in leave-one-out cross-validation with a Pearson correlation of 0.8 between the observed and fitted values and a mean absolute error of 8% (Figure 2C).
evidence: Direct statement of model validation results.

claim: 1.6% (95% CI: 1.5–1.7%) of the susceptible population gets infected each year across the four serotypes.
source: Using a catalytic model to estimate the proportion seropositive by age, we estimated that 1.6% (95% CI: 1.5–1.7%) of the susceptible population gets infected each year across the four serotypes, equivalent to an average of 2.4 million annual infections (95% CI: 2.2–2.5 million) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct statement from catalytic model analysis.

claim: There are an average of 2.4 million annual dengue infections (95% CI: 2.2–2.5 million) in Bangladesh.
source: Using a catalytic model to estimate the proportion seropositive by age, we estimated that 1.6% (95% CI: 1.5–1.7%) of the susceptible population gets infected each year across the four serotypes, equivalent to an average of 2.4 million annual infections (95% CI: 2.2–2.5 million) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct statement from catalytic model analysis.

claim: Within the three major urban hubs of Dhaka, Chittagong and Khulna, 6.4% (95% CI: 5.4–7.6%) of the population gets infected annually with no differences by sex.
source: Within these hubs, 6.4% (95% CI: 5.4–7.6%) of the population gets infected annually with no differences by sex, whereas this drops to 1.0% (95% CI: 0.9–1.2%) for females outside these areas and 1.6% (95% 1.4%–1.8%) for males (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: Direct statement from catalytic model analysis stratified by location.

claim: Outside the three major urban hubs, 1.0% (95% CI: 0.9–1.2%) of females get infected annually.
source: Within these hubs, 6.4% (95% CI: 5.4–7.6%) of the population gets infected annually with no differences by sex, whereas this drops to 1.0% (95% CI: 0.9–1.2%) for females outside these areas and 1.6% (95% 1.4%–1.8%) for males (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: Direct statement from catalytic model analysis stratified by location and sex.

claim: Outside the three major urban hubs, 1.6% (95% CI: 1.4%–1.8%) of males get infected annually.
source: Within these hubs, 6.4% (95% CI: 5.4–7.6%) of the population gets infected annually with no differences by sex, whereas this drops to 1.0% (95% CI: 0.9–1.2%) for females outside these areas and 1.6% (95% 1.4%–1.8%) for males (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: Direct statement from catalytic model analysis stratified by location and sex.

claim: If only 20 communities had been visited, seropositivity estimates would have ranged from 13% to 37%.
source: We found that if we had only visited twenty communities, the seropositivity among the samples would have ranged from 13% to 37%, depending on the communities visited.
evidence: Direct statement from sensitivity analysis on sampling design.

claim: If 60 communities had been visited, the range of seropositivity estimates would have been 22–28%.
source: By contrast, had we visited 60 communities, the range would have been much smaller (22–28%), with similar results in the spatial models.
evidence: Direct statement from sensitivity analysis on sampling design.

claim: In spatial models with no covariates, the mean absolute error in predictions per community fell from 13.6% when 20 communities were sampled to 10.5% when 69 communities were sampled.
source: In spatial models with no covariates, the mean absolute error in the predictions per community fell from 13.6% when 20 communities were sampled to 10.5% when 69 communities were sampled, with a corresponding rise in the correlation between the observed and predicted seroprevalence from 0.39 to 0.81 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Direct statement from sensitivity analysis on sampling design.

claim: The correlation between observed and predicted seroprevalence rose from 0.39 to 0.81 as the number of sampled communities increased from 20 to 69.
source: In spatial models with no covariates, the mean absolute error in the predictions per community fell from 13.6% when 20 communities were sampled to 10.5% when 69 communities were sampled, with a corresponding rise in the correlation between the observed and predicted seroprevalence from 0.39 to 0.81 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Direct statement from sensitivity analysis on sampling design.

claim: Sampling fewer people per community had little effect on estimates, with performance similar if 20 people were sampled per location compared to 80.
source: We found that sampling fewer people per community had little effect on our estimates, with the performance of nationwide and community-level seropositivity similar if 20 people were sampled per location compared to 80 (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Direct statement from sensitivity analysis on sample size per community.

claim: Dengue virus is a flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, that is found across tropical and subtropical regions.
source: Dengue virus is a flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, that is found across tropical and subtropical regions and causes a range of disease manifestations, ranging from asymptomatic infection to death (Petersen et al., 2012).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to support the claim.

claim: Dengue causes a range of disease manifestations, ranging from asymptomatic infection to death.
source: Dengue virus is a flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, that is found across tropical and subtropical regions and causes a range of disease manifestations, ranging from asymptomatic infection to death (Petersen et al., 2012).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to support the claim.

claim: Bangladesh is the most densely populated country in the world outside of city states, with 146 million people living in an area under 150,000 km2.
source: Outside of city states such as Singapore, Bangladesh is the most densely populated country in the world with 146 million people living in an area under 150,000 km2.
evidence: Direct statement providing demographic context.

claim: Sporadic dengue cases were reported in Bangladesh in the 1960s.
source: Sporadic cases were reported in the 1960 s and a major outbreak occurred in 2000 (Rahman et al., 2002; Sharmin et al., 2015; Yunus et al., 2001), with clinical cases reported annually since then (Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Ministry of health and family Welfare, 2017).
evidence: Direct statement with citations to support historical context.

claim: A major dengue outbreak occurred in Bangladesh in 2000.
source: Sporadic cases were reported in the 1960 s and a major outbreak occurred in 2000 (Rahman et al., 2002; Sharmin et al., 2015; Yunus et al., 2001), with clinical cases reported annually since then (Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Ministry of health and family Welfare, 2017).
evidence: Direct statement with citations to support historical context.

claim: Clinical dengue cases have been reported annually in Bangladesh since 2000.
source: Sporadic cases were reported in the 1960 s and a major outbreak occurred in 2000 (Rahman et al., 2002; Sharmin et al., 2015; Yunus et al., 2001), with clinical cases reported annually since then (Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Ministry of health and family Welfare, 2017).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to support historical context.

claim: A seroprevalence of 80% has been observed in Dhaka.
source: However, our knowledge of dengue epidemiology in the country is largely restricted to Dhaka, where a seroprevalence of 80% has been observed (Dhar-Chowdhury et al., 2017), with the burden elsewhere unknown (Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Ministry of health and family Welfare, 2017).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to prior study.

claim: Serum samples were tested for antibodies against IgG dengue virus using PanBio indirect IgG ELISAs.
source: The samples were tested for antibodies against IgG dengue virus, which indicates historic infection, using PanBio indirect IgG ELISAs (Alere Inc, Massachusetts, USA).
evidence: Direct statement describing the laboratory method used.

claim: BG Sentinel traps were placed in eight randomly sampled households in each of the 70 participating communities during the first visit in 2014.
source: During the first visit in 2014, BG Sentinel traps (Biogents AG, Germany) were placed in eight randomly sampled households in each of the of the 70 participating communities.
evidence: Direct statement describing mosquito trapping methodology.

claim: Mosquito trapping was repeated from June 2015 to July 2015 in communities where no Aedes mosquitoes were found during the initial trapping.
source: To help ensure that communities where no Aedes mosquitoes were found during the initial mosquito trapping truly had no Aedes, mosquito trapping was repeated in these communities from June 2015 to July 2015 during which eight households were randomly selected to have sentinel traps placed in their homes for 24 hr and the traps and mosquitos were processed in the same way as they had been initially.
evidence: Direct statement describing additional mosquito surveillance.

claim: The study was approved by the icddr,b ethical review board (protocol number PR-14058).
source: This study was approved by the icddr,b ethical review board (protocol number PR-14058).
evidence: Direct statement of ethical approval.

claim: The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention relied on icddr,b's ethical review board approval.
source: The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention relied on icddr,b's ethical review board approval.
evidence: Direct statement of ethical approval process.

claim: All adult participants provided written, informed consent after receiving detailed explanation of the study and procedures.
source: All adult participants provided written, informed consent after receiving detailed explanation of the study and procedures.
evidence: Direct statement of consent procedures.

claim: Parents/guardians of all child participants were asked to provide written, informed consent on their behalf.
source: Parents/guardians of all child participants were asked to provide written, informed consent on their behalf.
evidence: Direct statement of consent procedures for children.

claim: Serum was obtained from 76% of household members of participating households.
source: We obtained serum from 76% of household members of participating households (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing participation rate.

claim: Per community there were an average of 95 participants (range 81–116) from 20 households (range 20–23).
source: Per community there were an average of 95 participants (range 81–116) from 20 households (range 20–23).
evidence: Direct statement describing sample characteristics.

claim: The age and sex distributions in the study largely matched those obtained by the 2011 census although there was some under-representation in those <10 years.
source: The age and sex distributions in the study largely matched those obtained by the 2011 census although we had some under-representation in those <10 years (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement comparing study sample to census data.

claim: The PanBio assay appeared to discriminate well between those with and without past dengue infection.
source: The PanBio assay appeared to discriminate well between those with and without past dengue infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing assay performance.

claim: All communities had at least one seropositive individual.
source: While all communities had at least one seropositive individual, there was substantial spatial heterogeneity across the country with the proportion seropositive ranging from 3% in rural Maulvibazar in Sylhet Division to 88% in urban Chittagong.
evidence: Direct statement describing the distribution of seropositivity.

claim: Within Dhaka district, seropositivity ranged from 36 to 85% across three urban communities.
source: Even within Dhaka district (which includes the capital and has the highest population density), where we visited three urban ('Thana') communities, there was substantial heterogeneity, with seropositivity ranging from 36 to 85%.
evidence: Direct statement describing heterogeneity within Dhaka.

claim: The two urban communities visited in the city of Chittagong had seropositivities of 84 and 88%.
source: The two urban communities we visited in the city of Chittagong had seropositivities of 84 and 88%.
evidence: Direct statement describing seropositivity in Chittagong.

claim: The difference in seropositivity between males and females was concentrated in communities where overall seropositivity was <20%.
source: In particular, males were much more likely to be seropositive (odds ratio [OR]: 1.6 [95%CI: 1.4–1.9]; adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 1.7 [1.5–2.0]), although this difference was concentrated in communities where overall seropositivity was <20% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figure showing stratified analysis.

claim: The estimated number of seropositive individuals in Bangladesh (40.3 million) is much less than the 16.7 million previously estimated through a modelling exercise.
source: Overall, we estimated that around a quarter of the population, around 40 million individuals, have been infected by dengue with an average of 2.4 million annual infections. This figure is much less than the 16.7 million previously estimated through a modelling exercise (Bhatt et al., 2013), highlighting the need for representative data to help support these models and the importance of considering immunity in the estimation of annual case numbers.
evidence: Direct comparison with prior modeling study with citation.

claim: Dengue has only established a pattern of sustained endemic transmission in a few urban settings in Bangladesh, not throughout the country.
source: Our results suggest that since dengue re-emerged in the late 1990 s, the virus has only established a pattern of sustained endemic transmission in a few urban settings, and not throughout the country, as is the case in nearby Myanmar, Thailand and Cambodia (Rahman et al., 2002; Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Ministry of health and family Welfare, 2017; van Panhuis et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement with citations comparing to neighboring countries.

claim: The limited presence of Ae. aegypti may be part of the reason dengue has not established sustained endemic transmission throughout Bangladesh.
source: Part of the reason for this may be the limited presence of the principal vector, Ae. aegypti, which was found in only one third of the communities that participated in this study.
evidence: Direct statement linking vector presence to transmission patterns.

claim: The negative correlation between Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus presence is consistent with the species occupying different environmental niches or competition between the two species.
source: Our finding of a negative correlation between Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus presence is consistent with the species occupying different environmental niches or competition between the two species, as has previously been suggested (Braks et al., 2004).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to support interpretation.

claim: All communities had at least one seropositive individual, suggesting that external viral introductions may be common.
source: All communities had at least one seropositive individual, suggesting that external viral introductions may be common and that there may be factors preventing large-scale outbreaks, including from the limited abundance of the Ae. aegypti vector.
evidence: Direct statement with inference about transmission dynamics.

claim: Comparing infection proportions between males and females can be a good marker of local dengue endemicity.
source: At the individual level, we found that males had 1.6 times the odds of having been infected as females, although this difference was concentrated in communities where overall seropositivity was low, suggesting that comparing infection proportions between males and females can be a good marker of local dengue endemicity.
evidence: Direct statement with inference from observed patterns.

claim: Individuals from communities with low or no transmission are likely to get infected when they travel to higher transmission areas.
source: These findings suggest that in the current scenario in which infection risk is heterogeneously distributed around the country, individuals from communities with low or no transmission are likely to get infected when they travel to higher transmission areas.
evidence: Direct statement with inference from travel and seropositivity associations.

claim: If the vector presence expands throughout Bangladesh, individuals who travel could act as sources of outbreaks within their home communities.
source: If the vector presence expands throughout the country, these individuals could act as sources of outbreaks within these communities.
evidence: Direct statement speculating about future transmission dynamics.

claim: The findings for dengue in Bangladesh are in marked contrast to what has been observed with chikungunya, where women were at significantly increased risk of infection.
source: Our findings are in marked contrast to what has been observed with chikungunya in Bangladesh, where women in a community that had a widespread chikungunya epidemic were found to be at significantly increased risk of being infected compared to males, with the increased risk of infection linked to greater time spent in and around the home (Salje et al., 2016b).
evidence: Direct comparison with prior study on chikungunya with citation.

claim: It may be difficult to generalize inferences across arboviruses due to differences in vector species and the frequency of introductions and risk of onwards spread.
source: These findings suggest that it may be difficult to generalize inferences across arboviruses due to differences in vector species and the frequency of introductions and risk of onwards spread.
evidence: Direct statement with inference from comparison of dengue and chikungunya findings.

claim: Incorporating spatial correlation into risk factor regression analyses only resulted in a relatively small improvement in model fit compared to hierarchical models with random intercepts at the community and household levels.
source: While we incorporated spatial correlation into our risk factor regression analyses, in practice this only resulted in a relatively small improvement in model fit compared to hierarchical models with random intercepts at the community and household levels.
evidence: Direct statement describing model comparison results.

claim: The biggest impact of incorporating spatial correlation was to move the coefficient estimate for Ae. aegypti presence towards the null.
source: The biggest impact of incorporating the spatial correlation was to move the coefficient estimate for Ae. aegypti presence towards the null.
evidence: Direct statement describing the effect of spatial correlation on coefficient estimates.

claim: The spatial covariance structure is a better predictor than basic mosquito absence/presence data because it is driven by and absorbs the true underlying environmental drivers including mosquito distributions.
source: This suggests that the covariance structure is a better predictor than the basic mosquito absence/presence data as the covariance is driven by, and absorbs, the true underlying environmental drivers including mosquito distributions.
evidence: Direct statement with inference about the role of spatial covariance.

claim: The crude estimate of the proportion seropositive in Bangladesh (24%) was very close to modelled estimates that incorporated age, sex and population distribution (25%).
source: While there was substantial spatial heterogeneity in the risk of being seropositive across the country, ultimately our crude estimates of the proportion seropositive in the country (24%) was very close to modelled estimates that incorporated the age, sex and population distribution in the country (25%).
evidence: Direct comparison of crude and modeled estimates.

claim: The close agreement between crude and modeled estimates provides strong support for the sampling frame used to capture population-level estimates of population exposure.
source: This provides strong support for the sampling frame we used to capture population-level estimates of population exposure.
evidence: Direct statement with inference about sampling design validity.

claim: Incorporating covariates (e.g., sex, age, population distribution) did not result in substantive improvements in predictive accuracy compared to models that included a spatial covariance term only.
source: Incorporating covariates (e.g., sex, age, population distribution) did not result in substantive improvements in predictive accuracy compared to models that included a spatial covariance term only.
evidence: Direct statement comparing model performance.

claim: The importance of spatial dependence is highlighted for obtaining accurate estimates in unsampled locations.
source: This highlights the importance of spatial dependence in obtaining accurate estimates in unsampled locations.
evidence: Direct statement with inference from model comparison.

claim: For the Dengvaxia vaccine, the WHO has recommended that countries perform nationally representative serosurveys to inform vaccine rollout.
source: For the only currently licensed vaccine, Dengvaxia, the WHO has recommended that countries perform nationally representative serosurveys to inform vaccine rollout as the vaccine only provides protection in people with existing antibodies (World Health Organization, 2016).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to WHO recommendation.

claim: Dengvaxia only provides protection in people with existing antibodies.
source: For the only currently licensed vaccine, Dengvaxia, the WHO has recommended that countries perform nationally representative serosurveys to inform vaccine rollout as the vaccine only provides protection in people with existing antibodies (World Health Organization, 2016).
evidence: Direct statement with citation about vaccine characteristics.

claim: The vaccination of seronegative individuals with Dengvaxia has been linked to increased risk of subsequent severe disease.
source: The vaccination of seronegative individuals has been linked to increased risk of subsequent severe disease (Salje et al., 2018; Hadinegoro et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement with citations to support vaccine safety concern.

claim: Any dengue vaccine rollout in Bangladesh should be concentrated to the urban areas of Dhaka, Chittagong and Khulna.
source: For Bangladesh, our findings suggest that any vaccine rollout should be concentrated to the urban areas of Dhaka, Chittagong and Khulna.
evidence: Direct statement with inference from seropositivity findings.

claim: Even in the urban areas of Dhaka, Chittagong and Khulna, the proportion seropositive at age 9 years is far below the 80% threshold where vaccine rollout is potentially feasible without pre-vaccination screening.
source: However, even in these communities, the proportion seropositive at age 9 years is far below the threshold of 80% where vaccine rollout is potentially feasible without pre-vaccination screening (World Health Organization, 2018).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to WHO threshold.

claim: Any dengue vaccine rollout in Bangladesh will require screening of individuals for presence of antibodies before vaccination.
source: Therefore, any rollout will require the screening of individuals for presence of antibodies before vaccination to avoid placing large numbers of individuals at risk for more severe disease manifestations.
evidence: Direct statement with inference from seropositivity findings and vaccine characteristics.

claim: Cross-reactivity of antibodies is a problem for all seroprevalence studies, especially with flaviviruses.
source: Cross-reactivity of antibodies is a problem for all seroprevalence studies, especially with flaviviruses.
evidence: Direct statement about methodological limitation.

claim: Cross-reactivity prevents quantifying the relative importance of the different dengue serotypes.
source: This prevents us from quantifying the relative importance of the different dengue serotypes.
evidence: Direct statement about study limitation.

claim: Some seropositive individuals may have been infected with Japanese encephalitis rather than dengue.
source: In addition, some seropositive individuals may have been infected with Japanese encephalitis rather than dengue.
evidence: Direct statement about potential cross-reactivity.

claim: Japanese encephalitis is typically only found in rural communities where it circulates at low levels (estimated at 2.7 cases/100,000).
source: However, Japanese encephalitis is typically only found in rural communities where it circulates at low levels (estimated at 2.7 cases/100,000) (Paul et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement with citation about Japanese encephalitis epidemiology.

claim: The number of false positives from Japanese encephalitis cross-reactivity is likely to be small because only low levels of dengue seropositivity were estimated in rural communities.
source: As we estimated only low levels of dengue seropositivity in rural communities, the number of false positives from Japanese encephalitis cross-reactivity is likely to be small.
evidence: Direct statement with inference about the impact of cross-reactivity.

claim: Around 90% of households that were approached agreed to take part in the study.
source: Around 90% of households that we approached agreed to take part in the study.
evidence: Direct statement about participation rate.

claim: BG sentinel traps have been shown to be well suited to trapping Aedes mosquitoes.
source: We used BG sentinel traps that have been shown to be well suited to trapping Aedes mosquitoes (Maciel-de-Freitas et al., 2006; Obenauer et al., 2010).
evidence: Direct statement with citations supporting trap choice.

claim: All communities where Aedes mosquitoes were not found in the initial visit were revisited for additional mosquito trapping.
source: In addition, we revisited all communities where we did not find Aedes mosquitoes in the initial visit for additional mosquito trapping.
evidence: Direct statement describing additional surveillance effort.

claim: Given the heterogeneous nature of mosquito distributions within communities, Aedes mosquitoes may have been missed in some communities where they breed.
source: However, given the heterogeneous nature of mosquito distributions within communities, we may have nevertheless failed to find Aedes mosquitoes in communities where they breed.
evidence: Direct statement acknowledging potential limitation.

claim: If Aedes mosquitoes were missed in some communities, Aedes may be more widespread than found in this study.
source: This would mean that Aedes may be more widespread than we found.
evidence: Direct statement with inference about potential underestimation.

claim: Simply asking people about whether or not they had been infected with dengue was not informative of past infection.
source: We found that simply asking people about whether or not they had been infected with dengue was not informative of past infection.
evidence: Direct statement about the limitation of self-reported data.

claim: Studies that only use questionnaires can only provide limited burden information for pathogens such as dengue.
source: This highlights that studies that only use questionnaires can only provide limited burden information for pathogens such as dengue.
evidence: Direct statement with inference from self-report findings.

claim: Demographic Health Surveys could benefit significantly from adding a serological component to their studies.
source: For example, Demographic Health Surveys, which collect detailed health questionnaires from randomly selected individuals across many countries could benefit significantly from adding a serological component to their studies.
evidence: Direct statement with inference about improving survey methods.

claim: In Bangladesh, where dengue is still emerging, surveillance for vectors could be a way to monitor risk of future outbreaks.
source: In Bangladesh, where dengue is still emerging, surveillance for vectors could be a way to monitor risk of future outbreaks and continued efforts to understand drivers of transmission could point to interventions to reduce its geographic spread.
evidence: Direct statement with inference about surveillance strategies.

claim: Nationally representative serum banks are a powerful tool for public health agencies to understand pathogen circulation patterns, vaccination levels, and the existence of spatial pockets of susceptibility.
source: By tracking the levels of pathogen-specific antibodies in populations, these banks are a powerful tool for public health agencies to understand a wide range of factors that can assist in the fight against diseases, including pathogen circulation patterns, vaccination levels, and the existence of spatial pockets of susceptibility (De Melker and Conyn-van Spaendonck, 1998; Gidding et al., 2005; Osborne et al., 2000).
evidence: Direct statement with citations supporting the utility of serum banks.

claim: To date, the accumulation and use of nationally representative banked sera have focused almost exclusively on vaccine preventable childhood infections.
source: To date, the accumulation and use of nationally representative banked sera have focused almost exclusively on vaccine preventable childhood infections.
evidence: Direct statement about historical focus of serum banks.

claim: Serum banks have the potential to be invaluable in efforts to understand the burden from arboviruses and optimize efforts for control, including the targeted deployment of vaccines.
source: However, serum banks also have the potential to be invaluable in efforts to understand the burden from arboviruses and optimize efforts for control, including the targeted deployment of vaccines (Imai and Ferguson, 2018).
evidence: Direct statement with citation about potential applications.

claim: High levels of subclinical infection and frequent clinical misclassification mean that even in locations with good disease surveillance, the underlying risk of dengue infection is poorly understood.
source: In these diseases, high levels of subclinical infection and frequent clinical misclassification mean that even in locations with good disease surveillance, the underlying risk of infection is poorly understood (Halstead, 2007).
evidence: Direct statement with citation about challenges in dengue surveillance.

claim: Studies that collect serum for the detection of pathogen-specific antibodies typically rely on either convenience samples or focus on single communities, often in major cities or where the perceived risk of the pathogen is believed to be greatest.
source: Studies that collect serum for the detection of pathogen-specific antibodies typically rely on either convenience samples (e.g., blood donations) or focus on single communities, often in major cities or where the perceived risk of the pathogen is believed to be greatest (Petersen et al., 2012; Salje et al., 2016a; Rodríguez-Barraquer et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct statement with citations about typical serostudy designs.

claim: The ability to generalize results from convenience samples or single-community studies to the wider population is rarely known.
source: While they are often a good starting place for understanding historic pathogen circulation in the sampled communities and age-groups, the ability to generalize the results to the wider population is rarely known.
evidence: Direct statement about limitations of typical serostudy designs.

claim: If communities are randomly chosen from across a country, we can estimate national incidence rates, the underlying spatial heterogeneity in burden, the spatial dependence across neighbouring communities and identify risk factors for infection.
source: By contrast, if communities are randomly chosen from across a country, we can estimate national incidence rates, the underlying spatial heterogeneity in burden, the spatial dependence across neighbouring communities and identify risk factors for infection.
evidence: Direct statement about advantages of nationally representative sampling.

claim: Nationally representative study designs provide mechanistic insights into pathogen spread and facilitate the development of data-informed control policies.
source: Such study designs therefore provide mechanistic insights into pathogen spread and facilitate the development of data-informed control policies.
evidence: Direct statement about benefits of nationally representative designs.

claim: Transmission of arboviruses, such as dengue, appears to be driven by the interplay of individual-, household-, and community-level factors.
source: Transmission of arboviruses, such as dengue, appears to be driven by the interplay of individual- (e.g., sex, age, travel), household- (e.g., water supply, use of mosquito control) and community-level (e.g., urban/rural, mosquito abundance) factors (Salje et al., 2016b; Rodríguez-Barraquer et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement with citations about transmission dynamics.

claim: To make data-informed decisions on how best to control dengue spread, we need to understand the relative importance of different factors by collecting detailed data across individual, household, and community scales.
source: In order to make data-informed decisions on how best to control spread, we need to understand the relative importance of these different factors by collecting detailed data across these scales.
evidence: Direct statement about data needs for control strategies.

claim: A recent literature search found only one nationally representative dengue seroprevalence study, from Singapore, but there was only a subset of age-groups considered.
source: A recent literature search found only one nationally representative dengue seroprevalence study, from Singapore, but there was only a subset of age-groups considered (Imai et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement with citation about prior nationally representative studies.

claim: In rural locations in Bangladesh (around three-quarters of the country), census-communities consist of villages, whereas in urban places, these communities are city wards.
source: In rural locations (around three-quarters of the country), these census-communities consist of villages, whereas in urban places, these communities are city wards.
evidence: Direct statement describing community definitions.

claim: The study team spent at least 5 days in each community during each visit.
source: For each visit, the study team spent at least 5 days in the community.
evidence: Direct statement describing field procedures.

claim: Data collection for a community was considered complete when at least 40 serum samples from at least 10 households had been collected.
source: Data collection for a community was considered to be complete when at least 40 serum samples from at least 10 households had been collected.
evidence: Direct statement describing sampling targets.

claim: Residents were offered a test to determine their blood group as a benefit of participating.
source: Residents were offered a test to determine their blood group as a benefit of participating.
evidence: Direct statement describing participant incentive.

claim: A phlebotomist collected 5 ml of venous blood from all individuals who gave consent.
source: A phlebotomist collected 5 ml of venous blood from all individuals who gave consent.
evidence: Direct statement describing sample collection procedure.

claim: Individuals who were sick at the time of blood collection were ineligible.
source: Individuals who were sick at the time were ineligible.
evidence: Direct statement describing exclusion criteria.

claim: Blood samples were centrifuged in the field and the serum extracted into separate vials before being shipped to icddr,b laboratories in Dhaka in nitrogen dry shippers.
source: These samples were centrifuged in the field and the serum extracted into separate vials before being shipped to icddr,b (previously known as the international centre for diarrhoeal disease research, Bangladesh) laboratories in Dhaka in nitrogen dry shippers.
evidence: Direct statement describing sample processing and transport.

claim: The study used hierarchical models with random intercepts for household and community to account for clustering.
source: For each covariate, we initially performed simple logistic regression to explore associations with dengue serostatus using a hierarchical model with random intercepts for household and community.
evidence: Direct statement describing statistical methods.

claim: The study accounted for spatial correlation structure using a Matern covariance function using a stochastic partial differential equation.
source: We accounted for spatial correlation structure using a Matern covariance function using a stochastic partial differential equation and fitted the models using integrated nested Laplace approximations (INLA) in a Bayesian framework (Lindgren et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement describing statistical methods with citation.

claim: Models were fitted using integrated nested Laplace approximations (INLA) in a Bayesian framework.
source: We accounted for spatial correlation structure using a Matern covariance function using a stochastic partial differential equation and fitted the models using integrated nested Laplace approximations (INLA) in a Bayesian framework (Lindgren et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement describing statistical methods with citation.

claim: A sensitivity model was performed using only individuals > 20 years to assess whether results were affected by age-related differences in past dengue circulation.
source: As the probability of being seropositive is strongly linked to the past circulation of dengue, we also performed a sensitivity model in which we recalculated the regressions using only individuals > 20 years as seropositivity was not found to differ by age among older adults.
evidence: Direct statement describing sensitivity analysis.

claim: A 5 km x 5 km grid was placed over Bangladesh to estimate the population size in each grid cell using data from worldpop.org.
source: To explore the variability in dengue risk across Bangladesh, we initially placed a 5 km x 5 km grid over the country and estimated the population size in each of those grid cells using data available from worldpop.org (Tatem, 2017).
evidence: Direct statement describing spatial prediction methodology with citation.

claim: The fitted spatial prediction model was used to predict in unsampled grid cells by drawing 1000 samples from the posterior for each grid cell.
source: We used the fitted model to predict in the unsampled grid cells by drawing 1000 samples from the posterior for each grid cell and calculated the mean as well as 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles to quantify uncertainty.
evidence: Direct statement describing prediction methodology.

claim: The estimated number of seropositive individuals in a grid cell was calculated by multiplying the estimated proportion seropositive in a cell by the population within that cell.
source: The estimated number of seropositive individuals in a cell was calculated by multiplying the estimated proportion seropositive in a cell by the population within that cell.
evidence: Direct statement describing calculation method.

claim: The total number of seropositive individuals in Bangladesh was calculated as the sum of seropositive individuals across all the grid cells.
source: The total number of seropositive individuals in the country was calculated as the sum of seropositive individuals across all the grid cells.
evidence: Direct statement describing calculation method.

claim: A sensitivity analysis predicted the spatial distribution of dengue seropositivity using a model with the Matern spatial covariance matrix only (without any covariates).
source: As a sensitivity analysis, we also predicted the spatial distribution of dengue seropositivity in the country using a model with the Matern spatial covariance matrix only (i.e., without any covariates).
evidence: Direct statement describing sensitivity analysis.

claim: Four different models were assessed for their ability to accurately predict the level of seropositivity in unsampled locations: crude proportion seropositive, multivariable logistic model with spatial covariance, multivariable logistic model without spatial dependence, and spatial dependence model with no covariates.
source: We considered four different models: (i) crude proportion seropositive, (ii) multivariable logistic model with sex, age-group and population size as covariates and Matern spatial covariance (the baseline model), (iii) multivariable logistic model with sex, age-group and population size as covariates but with no spatial dependence, and (iv) spatial dependence model using Matern spatial covariance with no covariates.
evidence: Direct statement describing model comparison approach.

claim: For model validation, subsets of communities were repeatedly randomly selected to train the model (varied between 2, 20, 40, 60 and 69 communities) and seroprevalence was predicted in the remaining communities.
source: For 100 iterations and for each model in turn, we repeatedly randomly selected a subset of communities to train the model (varied between 2, 20, 40, 60 and 69 communities) and predicted the seroprevalence in the remaining communities not used to fit the model.
evidence: Direct statement describing validation methodology.

claim: The study assessed the impact of sampling fewer people per community by rerunning models with between 2 and 80 individuals sampled per community.
source: Separately, we considered the impact of having sampled fewer people per community. We reran each of the four models over repeated iterations using 50 randomly selected communities and with between 2 and 80 individuals sampled per community to train the models.
evidence: Direct statement describing sensitivity analysis on sample size.

claim: Catalytic models were used to estimate the proportion of the susceptible population that get infected each year using the probability of being seropositive as a function of age.
source: We used the probability of being seropositive as a function of age to estimate the proportion of the susceptible population that get infected each year using catalytic models, an approach which has been used frequently to reconstruct the past circulation of pathogens (Salje et al., 2016a; Rodríguez-Barraquer et al., 2014; Imai et al., 2015; Ferguson et al., 1999).
evidence: Direct statement describing analytical approach with citations.

claim: The catalytic model assumed a constant force of infection due to all four serotypes and that there were no differences in risk by age.
source: We assumed a constant force of infection due to all four serotypes, λ and that there were no differences in risk by age.
evidence: Direct statement describing model assumptions.

claim: The number of years prior to 2014 that dengue has circulated in Bangladesh (NYears) was fixed at 20 years.
source: We fixed NYears at 20 to reflect the approximate period when dengue first appeared in the country.
evidence: Direct statement describing model parameter.

claim: A sensitivity analysis varied the number of years dengue has circulated (NYears) between 15 and 25 years.
source: We conducted a sensitivity analysis where this was varied between 15 and 25 years.
evidence: Direct statement describing sensitivity analysis.

claim: The force of infection was calculated separately by sex and for the three largest cities versus the rest of the country.
source: We calculated the force of infection for the entire sampled population as well as separate estimates by sex and for the locations from the three largest cities (Dhaka, Chittagong and Khulna) only versus the rest of the country.
evidence: Direct statement describing stratified analyses.

claim: To estimate the number of people infected each year, the study used the estimated population by age for each year for the period 1995–2014.
source: To estimate the number of people infected each year we used the estimated population by age for each year for the period 1995–2014 (Kinsella and He, 2009).
evidence: Direct statement describing data source with citation.

claim: The model assumed that in 1995, the entire population was susceptible to dengue.
source: We assumed that in 1995, the entire population was susceptible.
evidence: Direct statement describing model assumption.

claim: The serotype specific force of infection was calculated as λ/4.
source: The proportion of the population that have monotypic immunity is calculated as w(a,y)=4 x exp(−3 x λs x a*) x (1-exp(-λs x a*)) where λs is the serotype specific force of infection and is calculated as λ/4
evidence: Direct statement describing calculation method.

claim: The study estimated the number of primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary dengue infections.
source: Using these proportions we can calculate the number of primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary dengue infections.
evidence: Direct statement describing model outputs.

claim: The estimated total number of infections presented includes primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary infections.
source: We present the estimated total number of infections across primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary infections.
evidence: Direct statement describing what is included in estimates.

claim: There has been growing recognition of the utility of nationally representative serum banks to monitor the burden from infectious diseases in a population.
source: There has been growing recognition of the utility of nationally representative serum banks to monitor the burden from infectious diseases in a population (Metcalf et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2012; Osborne et al., 1997; Jardine et al., 2010; De Melker and Conyn-van Spaendonck, 1998; van der Klis et al., 2009).
evidence: Direct statement with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: The optimal number of communities to visit will depend on the size and distribution of the population, the underlying level and heterogeneity of infection in the population, the required level of precision and the available budget.
source: The optimal number of communities to visit will depend on the size and distribution of the population, the underlying level and heterogeneity of infection in the population, the required level of precision and the available budget.
evidence: Direct statement about factors affecting study design.

claim: The finding that spatial correlation exists within 100 km suggests that communities should be sampled at a density to ensure that there is at least one sampled community within 100 km of all residents.
source: However, our finding that spatial correlation exists within 100 km suggests that communities should be sampled at a density to ensure that there is at least one sampled community within 100 km of all residents and preferably more.
evidence: Direct statement with inference about sampling design implications.

claim: There are fewer budget and time constraints to sampling additional individuals within a community than visiting additional communities.
source: Sampling as few as 20 individuals per community still provides robust nationwide estimates, however, in practice, there are fewer budget and time constraints to sampling additional individuals within a community than visiting additional communities.
evidence: Direct statement about practical considerations in study design.

claim: More detailed measures of movement (from e.g., movement diaries, global positioning system monitors) would help provide a more detailed understanding of how people move.
source: While this is likely to broadly capture trends in mobility, it remains a crude marker and more detailed measures of movement (from e.g., movement diaries, global positioning system monitors) would help provide a more detailed understanding of how people move.
evidence: Direct statement about potential methodological improvements.

claim: In cultural contexts where marriage rates may vary by community or location within a community, the method of choosing a random starting point based on recent weddings could produce a biased sample.
source: However, in cultural contexts where marriage rates may vary by community or location within a community, this method of choosing a random starting point could produce a biased sample.
evidence: Direct statement about potential limitation of sampling method.

claim: Given that >95% of adults marry in Bangladesh, it is unlikely that the approach of using recent weddings to identify a starting point could bias the sample obtained.
source: Therefore, we used a quasi-random approach that identified a starting point for household sampling based on the area of the community where the most recent wedding took place; given that >95% of adults marry in Bangladesh, it is unlikely that this approach could bias the sample we obtained.
evidence: Direct statement with inference about sampling method validity in Bangladesh context.
